I am a woman in my late forties, I reckon — old enough to have buried a parent and married off a daughter, young enough to still bend all day in the field. Twenty years I have farmed this same 1.8 mu in Quzhou, and I know every lump of it. I only went to primary school, so I do not read books about farming. I watch what happens on my own land, and I watch Old Wang’s family two plots over. If their wheat looks greener, I ask his wife what bag they bought.

My household has five mouths: my husband does odd construction work in the county town when he can, my son and his wife are in Shijiazhuang working in a factory, and my younger daughter still lives with us and helps when she is not at the village school. That means most days it is just me and my mother-in-law, who is nearly eighty but can still pick cotton. We have no money to hire labor. Every jiao I spend on inputs comes from the jar under the bed, and I need to leave some there for my mother-in-law’s medicine.

My land is tiny — 1.8 mu. I split it the way I have done for years: about 1.3 mu I keep for wheat and then maize right after, because that is how we eat. The other half-mu by the house I plant with cotton. It brings a little cash, and we use the cottonseed oil ourselves. I would not give up the cotton even though it is a lot of work, because when the grain price drops, that cotton money is what buys the salt and the soap.

**Wheat:** The wheat went in last October, same as always. I used improved seed — I buy it from the supply shop in the township, not the fancy hybrid stuff, just the regular improved variety that costs less and still gives decent grain. I put down some compound fertilizer at planting, about one small bag for the whole plot, and I will topdress with urea when the wheat turns green in March. I do not weigh it — I spread it by hand until the color looks right, but it is roughly what my neighbor uses, maybe a bit less because I am careful with money. I will irrigate three times: once at green-up, once when the wheat starts jointing, and once at filling stage if the sky gives us no rain. I always do rotary tillage before planting; the machine comes by the village and charges by the mu. For pests, I spray once for weeds and maybe twice more if I see aphids. I expect about 450 kg per mu — I got 480 two years ago, but last year was dry and I only got 420, so I am not greedy.

**Maize:** As soon as the wheat comes off in early June, I plant maize. There is no time to plough — nobody around here does. You harvest wheat, you drill maize the next day, no-tillage. I buy hybrid seed every year; you cannot save maize seed, everyone knows that. I put down a little urea at planting, not much, because the wheat stubble and roots are still in the ground and there is some fertility left. I irrigate twice if it does not rain — once to help it germinate if June is dry, and once at flowering in August. Two sprays: one herbicide, one for the corn borer if I see moths. I hope for 500 kg per mu. That is enough to feed the family and sell a little.

**Cotton:** I plant cotton on that half-mu in late April. I use improved seed, not the expensive Bt kinds — they cost too much for such a small patch. Cotton is hungry for spray. I will spray maybe eight or ten times through the season for bollworm, aphids, and weeds. It sounds like a lot, but if you skip even one spray on cotton, you lose the whole crop. I irrigate twice, and I put down a little urea when the plants start flowering. My mother-in-law picks it by hand in September and October. I expect about 280 kg of seed cotton per mu — it is sandy soil by the house, not as good as the main field.

Why do I do it this way? Because I have tried changing before and it cost me. Three years ago I put less urea on the wheat to save money, and the yield dropped so much I had to buy flour from the market. Never again. I would rather use a little too much and sleep easy. The cotton stays because it is my insurance — when the maize price is low, the cotton money is what gets us through the winter. And I do not plough for maize because there is no time, and because Old Wang tried ploughing once between wheat and maize and his maize came up a week late and never caught up. I learn from what I see.
